Government Orders
Having said that, I would like to thank members of the House for their co-operation.

Madam Speaker, I first apologize for not being a participant in this debate up to this point. Unfortunately I was attending a grain conference in Winnipeg when we found out at about two o'clock this morning that the assessment officer whom the Minister of Labour had sent to Thunder Bay to meet with both sides had failed to get both parties to agree on some form of a settlement and as a result the legislation that is before this House would be introduced this morning. Since it is very important to the grain industry in Thunder Bay I thought it my duty to return from that conference and attend to make some comments this afternoon with respect to this legislation.
Not to detract from what the minister has just stated and not to delay the passage of the bill, I want to assure him of that, but the remarks I am going to make concern some of the issues that affect the people who work in the grain industry in Thunder Bay.
During this whole unfortunate process I have spoken several times to both parties that were intimately involved in trying to reach a settlement. I think I should on their behalf explain to the House, and through the House perhaps to the people of Canada, the very issues that have stopped the flow of grain through the port of Thunder Bay for the last several days.
At the outset I think it is important to note that the grain workers in Thunder Bay are not selfish in what they have done. As we compare the grain workers in Thunder Bay with the grain workers in Prince Rupert and Vancouver, the grain workers in Thunder Bay are making something like $2.50 less an hour than their colleagues in Vancouver.
Coupled with that there is also the fact that the grain workers in Thunder Bay work approximately a six-month year, whereas their counterparts work up to a ten-month year. We can see that there is a substantial difference in the annual take-home pay of people who work in the same industry moving the same type of grain and, as I am told today, moving it to the same markets that traditionally were the markets serviced by the grain industry and the grain workers in Thunder Bay.

October 10, 1991
Government Orders
I will just relate a few personal incidents that I think are very important.
First and foremost, as the day approached we saw the veiy fine union representative, Herbert Daniher, in complete frustration at not being able to get the companies to sit down at the table and negotiate a contract. Although we may put fine words on it, the reason they did not want to negotiate was the fact that they made a pre-condition to sitting down at the table, stating that pensions were not to be discussed.
As it stands with this legislation now, it is very evident that when the conciliator-arbitrator is appointed after the passage of this bill, the mediator-arbitrator will certainly discuss the pension issue. I am certain that he will treat those people in the port of Thunder Bay with the degree of fairness that up to now they have not been treated with.
I also think of some of the incidents that have led up to this dispute, and I say that they are incidents that affect human beings working in a community that did not have to exist. I am thinking in particular of this summer and a man named John Pino coming into my office. He had worked for 15 and a half years for Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, had not been called back to work for the 18-month period, and had received his final termination from Saskatchewan Wheat Pool. This is a family man with responsibilities and a mortgage, like all of us. After dedicating 15-plus years to this elevator complex, he was told that his services were no longer needed, and this is the unfortunate part, because the grain was moving through the port of Thunder Bay and the people working at that elevator were working double and triple time and it chose to work people double and triple time rather than calling back these people who had 14 years and 15 years of seniority.
That is not fair play and that is the reason for the frustration in the grain industry in Thunder Bay today.
I think of people who have walked through my office in the last two or three months who were involved. Baldino Iello, whom I was at a hockey game with on Saturday night in Thunder Bay, contributed over 20 years of his life to this industry and finally gave up in frustration, saying that he could not carry on in the present circumstances any longer, mainly because the equity, the quality and the way some of these people are treated are no longer tolerable.
Those are just a couple of the human elements that I had dealt with throughout the summer. I think that is the unwritten agenda that has caused the frustration and the dilemma in which we find ourselves today.
There is no question in my mind as to what is needed. I would hope that the industrial commissioner Mr. Daniher has requested and whom the minister will appoint very shortly will continue after this legislation is in place and long after a settlement is reached by the mediator-arbitrator to look at what is happening in the grain industry, particularly in Thunder Bay, with respect to justice for its people, with respect to equity between the various parts of Canada, and with respect to consideration for the contribution which those people have worked long and hard in the grain industry in Canada to give. They should not be treated in the way they are being treated.
I would hope and would suggest to the minister that I hope the industrial commissioner he will appoint will be given a broad mandate in order to look into these injustices that have been perpetrated on the grain workers at Thunder Bay for so many years.
The dilemma they find themselves in is that five years ago we had over 2,400 employees working in the grain industry in Thunder Bay. Today there are fewer than 700 people working full time.
Of those 700 people there are usually 200 or 300 off on part-time work. In a period of five years that industry has gone from 2,500 down to less than 700. That is the whole substance. In essence, that is why we are here today passing back-to-work legislation to get the grain moving.
Let me also say that there is empathy on behalf of the grain workers in Thunder Bay for the farmers in Saskatchewan and Manitoba. I would want to address that issue for just a moment. I hope that those people who are on farms in Saskatchewan and Manitoba would not look unkindly to the people who are working in the grain industry in Thunder Bay because they face the same dilemma. The hardships that they are facing in the prairies today are much the same hardships that are being faced by the people who are working in the port of Thunder Bay.
October 10,1991

The price of wheat is not what it should be, neither are the wages. That leads me to the issues that I think are so important to bring before this House and before the people of Canada. These are the fundamental issues over which the companies have refused to sit down and negotiate on behalf of the employees who are being directly affected because of the huge loss of jobs that are happening on our waterfront. What we are trying to accomplish is just a certain amount of stability in that area of commerce so there can be planning, so they can go out and make the purchases necessary to house and cloth their families, and that is being denied to those people who work in that industry.
The issues, and we have heard the words, deal with pensions and what is called job security. I have taken those two issues, and they are almost buzzwords in the negotiating field today, and I have broken down them down into four elements with the help of my colleagues in Thunder Bay. Let me just explain for a few moments what those four issues are.
In the bargaining package they want what is called credited service. Because of the long terms of lay-offs, up to 18 months in some instances, when an employee who has worked for a considerable amount of years in the grain industry in Thunder Bay came to retire he may have 35 years of seniority but only 22 years of credited service because of the amount of time that he worked. All the employees want in this bargaining process is the ability to pay into their pension plan their regular contribution. It is not free. They want to be able to pay a voluntary contribution to their pension plan so that during the times they are unemployed because of lay-off they will be able to contribute to the pension plan and when it comes time to retire they will have 30 years of seniority, as an example, and 30 years of credited service.
When you compare this to any other industry, I do not care whether you are in mining or manufacturing automobiles or tires or working for the government, when you retire after 30 years you are usually credited with 30 years of pension. That has been denied the employees in the grain industry in Thunder Bay and that is just what they are asking for. It is that simple.
The other thing and part of the area that was not discussed was that they wanted to reduce the retirement age to 55 in order that they could bring the work force into some kind of balance, retiring those people with more seniority and bringing on fresh talent.
Presently the age is 58.1 think the figure that we use is
Government Orders
85: the age of the individual plus the number of years of seniority. If that equals 85 they are allowed to retire. They wanted the retirement age reduced to 55. The dilemma they find themselves in is that they could not negotiate-the company refused to negotiate-the difference between age 55 and age 58. Any one of us who has bargained at the bargaining table knows that you come in with one position on the one side and the other position, you sit down, and as long as you are talking to one another you are going to arrive at some kind of a settlement. You cannot arrive at a settlement if you are not going to sit down at the table and bargain. There is not a great deal of difference between a retirement age of 55 and a retirement age of 58. I think that is a non-issue that has led to this dilemma that we find ourselves in today because of the intransigence of the company in sitting down and negotiating these areas.
The other area-Madam Speaker, I know you are going to say this is trivial-is the benefits that an employee receives at the age of retirement. The employee who works in the grain industry is allowed at the end of the day, after fulfilling his terms of service which equal 85, to continue on with his drug plan as long as he agrees to pay $81 a month.
During the whole process of his employment he was on a dental plan. This is the crux of the argument here. As he approaches and decides on retirement, he no longer has the option to use the dental plan or participate in the dental plan after his retirement. That is just not fair.
When a person works in a company he is used to a drug plan and a dental plan as he is used to the other benefits. One of our Crown corporations, Canadian National Railways according to yesterday's The Globe and Mail, is one of the least competitive railways in North American according to research done by its own accounting firm. I suggest that we look at the benefits that these people receive and compare them to the benefits that these grain elevator workers receive in Thunder Bay.
In the last issue that prevented a settlement or even a negotiating point is something that they called income protection. There is not a great deal of job security when we talk about income protection. I do not want this to be misconstrued. This is not indexing as we know it and as I understand it. I am not in the pension plan of the government.

October 10, 1991
Government Orders
As I understand it, government pension plans in this very House are indexed according to inflation. I know among the school teaching profession that their pension plan is indexed to compensate for the cost of living. The elevator employees in Thunder Bay have never had the benefit of indexing in their pension plan.
What they have done and what happened up until 1984 was that the company would sit down with the union at the end of the year and say: "Yes, cost of inflation". They would negotiate for the pension plan something less than the normal inflationary rate that would allow the employee who had worked for the elevator company for a number of years to live with a certain amount of dignity.
In 1984 the company said: "That can no longer be the case. From here on in, in every bargaining process, we want what is called income protection on the table and we will bargain for it every year".
In 1988 they refused to bargain income protection so that the pensions that were paid in 1984 without any increase are the same pensions that are being paid in 1991.
All the union wanted was to have a certain amount of protection to say: "Will you look at the pension plan? We do not expect indexing. We are not asking for pie in the sky, but look at the pension plan and try to take into consideration some of the increased cost of living. Try to compensate us in some way toward achieving that goal". That is all that is. I do not see a great deal of job protection in that benefit.
Those are the issues. There are four issues: credited service, reduced retirement age to 55, minimum benefits on retirement, and income protection. Those are the only four issues that have caused the movement of grain to stop in the port of Thunder Bay mainly because the companies would not sit and negotiate.
They adopted the stance: "If you want to talk about pensions, we are not going to come and bargain". That is not fair. It is not fair to the work force and it is not fair to the system of bargaining and labour negotiations that we have come to expect in this country.
Therefore, I sympathize a great deal with the workers who I represent from the city of Thunder Bay. I know my party does not normally like to accept back-to-work legislation as we have seen it in this House. Given that the companies failed to respond, to sit down and bargain, I am satisfied-and I am sure my colleagues are satisfied-that the employees will finally be able to get a fair hearing with the assistance of the mediator-arbitrator who will be appointed immediately after this legislation is passed. At least there will be a certain amount of justice done on behalf of the employees who work in the grain industry in Thunder Bay.
I hope that is the essence of what we are doing here today for their benefit.

Madam Chairman, I thank the minister for defining a few minutes for me.
This is actually an historical debate for the city of Thunder Bay and for the port of Thunder Bay. It is the first time in 25 years that this House has found it necessary to legislate workers and/or the company back to work at the port of Thunder Bay. In the past the threat of legislation has been used effectively to force the parties to the bargaining table. This time, because of the new calendar of the House we are not sitting next week and I think the pressure was not appropriately applied in a way that would have brought forward the result of some kind of negotiations. I regret that.
I regret too the manner in which the workers in Thunder Bay have been attacked verbally by members of this House, ministers of the Crown, and representatives of certain groups in the prairies. I want to spend a bit of my time dispelling the myth that this particular strike taken by the members of the grain handling union in Thunder Bay was in some way punishing the farmers of western Canada.
We have seen headlines and news stories saying millions of dollars a day are lost because of the strike at Thunder Bay. One would assume that means that people have not been able to get the grain that they bought and therefore no money was coming into the system. We certainly know that it means that because the prairie elevators are full the farmer cannot deliver and therefore get paid. I grant that. However, in terms of the industry and in terms of the nation, two ships cleared the St. Lawrence River on October 4 and three ships cleared on October 7 carrying a combined total of 128,000 tonnes of grain that somebody was able to pick up and take to a customer. Madam Speaker, that suggests to me there has been no loss of sales. There has been no inability in this country to provide grain to its customers. Quite frankly, even if this rumoured $400 million sale to the Soviet Union is announced today or tomorrow, they are not going to be parked at Baie Comeau or Port Cartier or Quebec City tomorrow morning waiting to pick it up. Even if they do, assuming that the one million tonnes that is in storage in those downstream elevators is the right kind of grain, they could pick up some grains. So that we have not lost existing sales, we have not in any way impacted on our customers. And yes, some customers might want to wait to see how long it would take for the dispute to be resolved, but all they have to do is look back in history to know that in situations like this when
Government Orders
there is a lot of grain to move that at the most it is one or two weeks.
The other thing that people have to know, Madam Speaker, is that Thunder Bay has a remarkable ability to rebound. We were only scheduled to get 1,500 to 2,000 cars a week coming in from the prairies. We can do 6,000 a week without any question. We have been able to do much more than that. So we could recover very quickly. And if this legislation receives Royal Assent tomorrow, it is quite conceivable that the grain handlers and the elevator companies can be back at work on Saturday. The 5,000 cars that the Wheat Board has had filled, sitting on the rail tracks somewhere between Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Thunder Bay, if not a lot are parked in Thunder Bay, will very quickly be dumped into the elevators and the 16 or so ships that are sitting in the harbour will be quickly loaded and steaming downstream towards the transfer elevators.
So, Madam Speaker, we can recover. If the government believed that this strike really was causing harm to the farmers, it did not have to legislate the workers back to work. It would have been very simple to go, farm by farm, to where the country elevators were full and fill up
5,000	grain cars and use them for storage. I can understand if they decided not to fill up the total fleet of grain cars- I can understand why they would want some flexibility. But they decided to fill up only 5,000 cars and use them for storage out of a fleet of 26,000 cars. They could have added another 5,000 cars for storage, freeing up some space at the prairie elevators so that the farmers could have brought their grain from the farm gate to the elevator to get paid.
But they decided they didn't even want to do that. They could have taken the unusual step of going to the farm, determining how much was in storage, and providing a payment based on a pre-sale of that grain in storage so that the farmer would have the appropriate cash flow.
But this government did none of that. It did not attempt to find a way around the problem of moving grain off the farm gate. It also could have, starting next week-and I regret to say this- started moving grain from Manitoba and part of Saskatchewan to Vancouver. It could have also cleaned some of the grain out of the prairies and moved it by rail past Thunder Bay to Quebec City-something called the winter rail program, only this time it would be in the fall. It could have done those things if the issue really was to help the farmers. Of course, the reality is that if there had not been an election in Saskatchewan right now, if there had not been a massive crisis in the farm community where they

October 10, 1991
Government Orders
need $1.3 billion just to stay afloat, then perhaps the approach would have been different.
But this government I regret to say has been playing games with the lives of the people on the prairies and the lives of the people in the port of Thunder Bay.
Let us deal with the port for a second, Madam Speaker.
The Minister for Grains and Oilseeds is quoted in today's Globe and Mail as saying: "We are not going to sit by and see a port shut down that is a major part of our grain sales to one of our most important customers". He is reported to have said that at the rally at the Manitoba legislature yesterday.
Let us look at what has happened to the port of Thunder Bay since this government has taken office. At the outset I want to say that the initial cause is not its fault. It was the previous Liberal government that in 1983 passed what is now called the Western Grain Transportation Act which was the elimination of the Crow. In that act it provided a financial incentive to move a maximum amount of grain through the west coast at the expense of the port of Thunder Bay.
We have already been told that the number of grain handlers in Thunder Bay has gone from 1,700 in 1984 down to 700 today. That is 1,000 permanent well paid union jobs lost at the Lakehead.
We have also had the appropriate spin-off losses in rail. We have seen our Great Lakes shipping fleet cut in half in terms of the number of vessels we have. Madam Speaker, I want to say to you today if we have one of those bumper crops that we always dream about, this country can no longer move it to our customers should we have it. We no longer have the capacity to move 19 million tonnes out of the port of Thunder Bay throughout a year. We just cannot do it because of the neglect of the port of the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Seaway system.
I said at the outset that it was Liberal legislation that created the situation, but this government has been in
power since 1984. Seven years and there has been talk, talk, talk, but no action.
I just came back from a two-day conference in Winnipeg dealing with the issue of the direction of grain and how the WDTA is structured in terms of payments to the railroads or payment to the producers. I can tell you, Madam Speaker, that the frustration there was we have been talking about this and it is time for some action, time to restore some balance.
If the Minister for Grains and Oilseeds is sincere about the importance of the port of Thunder Bay, then it is time that this government got off its butt and did something to ensure that it has a permanent role in the movement of grain products from the prairies to export position, particularly to the Soviet Union. Most of the grain that goes to the Soviet Union comes through the port of Thunder Bay. A small portion goes through the port of Churchill and that is an issue as well that has to be addressed, to provide some permanency and stability to that grain community.
Madam Speaker, you have been told that the issues that have precipitated the strike are pensions and job security. I am not going to get into the details, the technical nature of it. I want to tell you the human side of it. If you have seen 1,000 of your colleagues lose then-jobs, if you have seen others who you have worked with for 15 to 20 years not have work for a year or a year and a half, if you had families who have lost their homes, marriages that have broke up because of the loss of employment, the loss of income, you can understand how important job security is to the people of the port of Thunder Bay.
This year has been a very bad year for us. We have lost one full paper mill with 400 plus people permanently out of work, another paper mill was downsized by over 400, a questionable future for UTDC, and thank heavens the province has stepped in to manage things until Lavalin can find a buyer so we can maintain that valuable rapid transit rail car construction facility in Thunder Bay. As we heard last week, our shipyard facility is doomed because of the lack of work for most shipyards in this country.
October 10, 1991

The strike has not been a good one. I do not blame the union for that. Everything that I saw leading up to it was a group of companies which wanted nothing more than to put their workers out on the street.
I want to give one example. On the Friday when the Public Service Alliance went back on the picket lines in Thunder Bay, one of the first groups to go back were the inspectors and the weighers.
I should tell you that the grain handlers union has a cause and a collective agreement which gives them the right to refuse to cross picket lines. Given that in the first phase of the PSAC strike, they did not cross the picket lines, one of the companies-I do not know which one-on the Monday after the PSAC lines were up again, had the nerve to call over 100 grain handlers back to work.
They called them off pogey, off unemployment insurance. They had to know that that meant they would lose unemployment insurance but not get any work because they could not cross the picket line. They would refuse to cross the picket line.
That is not fair bargaining. That is not setting a climate to provide for meaningful negotiations. The companies themselves have to accept the responsibility that they created the scenario that led to the walk-out by the grain handlers union.
I will just make a final few comments, because I realize that the time is running out. I want to say very clearly that I and my colleagues in this House will be saying "nay" when you ask if this legislation shall be passed. We will be voting against it because we do not believe that collective bargaining should be destroyed in this fashion.
I also want to make it clear that we are agreeable to see this legislation pass this House today, to be completed in this House today because we recognize that it will be futile from any point of view to continue this now that negotiations have failed.
Madam Speaker, let me leave you with one thought. Would we be doing this today if the House was sitting next week? I suspect not. I wonder once again about our priorities as we deal with these and other matters.

Madam Speaker, do you happen to own a fur coat?
Do not answer that, Madam Speaker, because I know that is a controversial subject these days. The animal rights activists, for instance, have understandable concerns about the humane trapping of animals although most of us still do eat meat and wear leather shoes.
It is really not because of the animal rights activists' concerns that the fur coat manufacturers are hurting these days, but they are hurting. Many of the fur coat
Adjournment Debate
manufacturers in Canada are Canadians of Greek origin. A great many of those live in my own constituency.
There are families such as the Papadopoulos family, the Zaphiropoulos family and the Frangos family, all of whom are involved in the production and the manufacture of fur coats in this country and have been for many years.
Four years ago, there were many animal rights activists around but the fur coat manufacturing business was a booming one. In fact, the Canadians of Greek origin who owned and operated those kinds of businesses in metropolitan Toronto made representations to me and to the Minister of Immigration to bring more skilled workers into the country to be able to help and assist them.
Their business was booming, and they needed more skilled labour. Many of them come from the region of kastoria in Greece. Today, they are in serious trouble and many of them are seeing a lifetime of effort just go down the drain. Others are hovering on the edge of disappearing altogether, and with them, thousands and thousands of jobs, jobs that are skilled jobs and high paying jobs.
The fur coat manufacturing industry is only one of many, many examples of the problems that we are facing today with the industry in southern Ontario and in metropolitan Toronto.
Since 1989, some 47 different industrial plants in metropolitan Toronto have closed finally and completely. Unemployment is now higher than the national average in metropolitan Toronto. It is now something like 10.8 per cent whereas just a year ago, it was 4.7 per cent.
Of the 85,000 people who are depending on general welfare assistance in metropolitan Toronto now, some
65,000	of them are employable if there were some jobs out there for them to be employed at. There are something like 127,000 residents of metropolitan Toronto now on unemployment insurance benefits.
This is virtually the worst situation in metropolitan Toronto since the Great Depression of the 1930s. In the early 1980s, we had a worse recession for Canada as a whole, but not for metropolitan Tbronto.
Now, metropolitan Toronto has been hit and it is hit hard by the economic downturn. There are programs in place as you know, Madam Speaker, to help Atlantic Canada, to help western Canada, and to help Quebec and northern Ontario.

October 10, 1991
Adjournment Debate
There is none for southern Ontario because southern Ontario and metropolitan Toronto have been traditionally considered as the fat cats. Perhaps they have been. Perhaps we have been in the past, but certainly we are not now.
For years and years, the former Liberal government and now our own government has had a policy that has provided little if any help for southern Ontario. Well, southern Ontario and metropolitan Toronto now need help, Madam Speaker, and I want to ask the minister tonight what he is going to do about it.

speechtext:
I would like to assure my hon. colleague that the federal government, in spite of what he said, is very active in southern Ontario. I would like to emphasize that we already have in place many policies and programs designed not only to prevent adverse economic development in southern Ontario, but also to provide the building blocks for long-term prosperity, not only in southern Ontario but for all Canadians from coast to coast.
Soon the government will launch its prosperity initiative and provide a forum in which Canadians can plan and work together to prepare for the challenge of a global economy.
In addition to concentrating on building long-term prosperity for southern Ontario, this government has already put in place many initiatives which benefit especially this part of the country. The program for export market development helps firms in Ontario to sell to border and southern states and the overseas market.
Southern Ontario firms benefit significantly from this assistance. I would like to also point out that the new exporters to the border states program has helped many southern Ontario firms get involved in the export market. So I think, Madam Speaker, that these initiatives and other federal initiatives and federal departments and agencies are playing an important role in supporting southern Ontario industries.
We realize on this side of the House, and my colleague is right in saying that there are problems in southern Ontario, as there are in many other parts of Canada, but the federal government is committed to helping the economy of those areas by providing means that will help the local economies of those areas and the local enterprises to grow and export and create jobs.

Madam Speaker, on September 18, in answer to my question, the hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs said that Canada considers that Indonesian sovereignty over East Timor is a fact. She also said that we do not condone the manner of incorporation and that we deplore and condemn the loss of life that occurred.
Apart from the fact that those statements seem not entirely consistent, I want to point out other contrary facts in the statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
Portugal is recognized by the United Nations as the administering power of East Timor and it has continued its dialogue in an attempt to resolve the state of invasion and oppression by Indonesia. It has recently sent a fact finding delegation and will soon send a parliamentary delegation to East Timor when the arrangements can be made.
It has taken Australia to the International Court of Justice for entering into a treaty with Indonesia to drill for East Timor's offshore oil.
Furthermore, Madam Speaker, on August 7 of this year, Amnesty International presented a 37-page report to the United Nations Special Committee on Decolonization in which they say, in part:
Serious violations continued to occur in East Timor over the last year, accelerating patterns of short-term detention, torture and ill-treatment of alleged political opponents, many of whom may be prisoners of conscience, and persistent reports of extra-judicial executions, hundreds of unresolved cases of disappearance and the continued imprisonment of at least nine alleged Fretelin supporters sentenced in trials which Amnesty International believes were unfair.
Not surprising, in spite of the Indonesian government statement that people are free to visit, Amnesty International has not been permitted to visit East Timor yet. Furthermore, Madam Speaker, our history does not have clean hands.
When our ambassador, Glen Shortliffe, advised the Canadian government that the takeover was a fait accompli, he also pointed out that this would result in greater benefits to Canadian companies in improved trading relations with Indonesia. That is what has happened. Over 300 companies have been investing in Indonesia, looking for the abundant natural resources, the tax holidays and the oppressed cheap labour earning no more than $1 U.S. per day.
October 10, 1991

Furthermore, Canada has provided arms to the Indonesian government that it used in continuing the oppression of the East Timorese people. In 1984 Canada assisted with a weapons bazaar in Indonesia and eight Canadian weapons manufacturers had facilities there. The list of companies that do business, and obviously find it profitable in Indonesia and East Timor, is too long to list, but it includes Air Canada, Alcan, Bank of Nova Scotia, Bell Aerospace, Canadian General Electric, Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas, International Nickel, West-inghouse, Litton Systems- a famous anti-labour, antiunion employer-and Levy Auto Parts Company.
I urge that the Secretary of State for External Affairs revise her understanding and reverse Canada's policy of supporting the aggressor, the invader and the oppressor, and work with Portugal to liberate by peaceful means through the United Nations the oppressed people of East Timor.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Canada considers that Indonesian sovereignty over East Timor is a fact, recognizing that there has never been any history of independence or self-government in the territory. Canada does not condone the manner of incorporation and deplores the loss of life that occurred. At the meeting of the UN Commission on Human Rights in February 1991 in Geneva, Canada expressed regret at the continued allegation of human rights abuses and urged Indonesia to ensure human rights are fully respected.
Canada expressed also its support for the Indonesian decision to open East Timor to domestic and international visitors.
Members of the Canadian Embassy in Jakarta make regular visits to East Timor to make inquiries on reports of human rights abuses, detentions, and the general living conditions pertaining there. The last visit took place in September. There are indications that tension is mounting in the wake of the visit of a Portuguese parliamentary delegation this month with possible consequences with respect to the human rights situation.
Adjournment Debate
Canada continues to closely follow the situation in East Timor, and of course we fully agree with the hon. member's concern for the human rights situation in this part of Indonesia.

Madam Speaker, I rise this evening to address a question that I had posed in the House September 26 to the President of the Treasury Board. The question was raised with regard to the amounts of bonuses that are being paid to certain managers in the Public Service and the senior executives of Crown corporations.
There was some discussion at the time, if I recall correctly, that they were bonuses and then they were not bonuses; they were Christmas bonuses but they are not Christmas bonuses; they are part of their pay package, they are being paid at Christmas time, but it is not really a Christmas bonus.
To this date we are still not too sure exactly what they are. The fact remains that a lot of these executive types are getting upwards of $85,000 and in some instances which I will refer to in a moment they can get as high as perhaps even $99,000, in the form of a pay bonus.
We have been told by the President of the Treasury Board that these are a recompense for productivity.
This is happening at a time when the hourly rated workers are being offered zero, three and three. I take offence to the fact that when I addressed the question the President of the Treasury Board referred to the fact that if zero per cent were such a fast number, why was it not good enough for PSAC. I think that is an insult to the workers who are the very people who produce, who make the boss "look good", the senior executives who are getting these fat cat bonuses off the backs of these very workers who are being told they are getting zero.
There is something wrong when we hear on one side that there is no money, that the funds have dried up, that we have to tighten our belts, that we all have to contribute, that it is not time to spend and give raises. It is time for restraint.

October 10,1991
Adjournment Debate
On the other hand we say that some time ago there was 15 per cent taken out of the wage package of these senior executives and it is only being given back to them in the form of a bonus if they are productive.
It is a contradiction in terms. They are not the ones who are being productive. It is the people on the front line who are productive. They are the ones who are producing.
In the last couple of days there have been some votes in this House with regard to forcing people back to work. PSAC was one group. The grain elevator operators are the other group.
If things come in threes I guess the next group of people who will be ordered back to work if they do go out on strike-and it looks as if they probably will-will be the postal workers.
We are told by the President of the Treasury Board that the bonuses and the wage structure are regulated by an advisory board. That advisory board has told the government that the Canada Post Corporation president's wages should be between $248,000 and $310,000. If we take an average of $300,000 and that executive is entitled to 25 per cent, because that is also the guideline, he will get $75,000 bonus.
My time is up but I would love to go on much longer.
The point remains that this whole idea of bonuses has to be reviewed and I am asking the minister to appoint a review board or send it to committee, but this double standard cannot go on. I am asking the minister to respond.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance); Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the principle of the compensation for senior executives is that their total compensation consists of two parts: base salary and performance pay.
Increases to their base salary were limited to 4.2 per cent for 1990-91, which is the same average increase awarded other public servants for the same period.
Similarly, collectively bargained employees whose agreements expired prior to the February 26 budget will receive a 4.2 per cent increase as provided for in Bill C-29.
With regard to performance pay for the Governor in Council community, including heads of Crown corporations, bonuses are only awarded based on performance in achieving corporate objectives. They have not yet been approved or paid for performance during the fiscal year
1990-	91.
I would like to add that bonuses for heads of Crown corporations are only awarded on recommendations of boards of directors.
This elaborate consultative and administrative process accounts for the delay in implementation.
The government rejects the view that the restraint measures should reach back to some people retroactively, for previous years' service, but not to others. This clearly would be unfair. The same principle should apply to everyone.
In keeping with the government's restraint program, performance pay has been suspended for the fiscal year
1991-	92 for all senior executives and Governor in Council appointees inclusive of the heads of Crown corporations. This combined with a wage freeze for 1991 means that senior level total compensation will be subject to zero increase in that year, similar to collectively bargained employees. I should add that for the latter, however, salary increments will continue to be paid during that period.
I would like you to know that senior level compensation is normally established on the basis of independent advice and recommendations to the Prime Minister from the advisory group on executive compensation in the Public Service. That group is made up of eight senior executives from the Canadian business community and has provided advice over the past 23 years to successive governments. They support performance pay for senior executives as an alternative and a more cost efficient and effective method of distributing compensation. I should add that this method of compensation is widely used in the private sector.
Finally, as the President of the Treasury Board has indicated time and time again, there will be no salary increases nor performance pay for fiscal year 1991-92 for members of the management category and Governor in Council appointees including the heads of Crown corporations.
October 10, 1991

Madam Speaker, two weeks ago in this House I directed a question to the Minister of Finance. It was answered by the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology. It had to do with Mr. Lou MacEachem who received the Entrepreneur of the Year Award in Calgary.
Upon receiving his award, Mr. MacEachem announced that because of the GST, the high dollar and other taxes, he was selling his business, and I said: "and leaving the country".
I asked the minister: When was this government going to stop drowning small business in red tape and taxes.
The minister, who is a skilled parliamentarian, was at the dinner and got up and said that Mr. MacEachem was not leaving the country. I naturally felt like the minister sort of blew me out of the water. I felt that my facts were not really correct.
Subsequently, I went and had a further chat with Mr. MacEachem who did receive the Entrepreneur of the Year Award. There are two points that I want to make. The first one is that the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology was right in that Mr. MacEachem himself is not leaving the country. But the real truth of the matter is that Mr. MacEachem, a man who employs over 300 people, is selling off his businesses. He wrote me a letter: "Further to our telephone conversation, Mr. Mills. If I had not received the Entrepreneur Award this year, it would never have happened to me in Canada because the entrepreneurial spirit has been killed in Canada by government and is dead in me so for as Canada is concerned".
He went on to mention that he showed the Minister for International Trade a number of articles, which he attached, as to what some of the problems were with taxes, red tape and paper burden in this country. He then went on to say: "Having started many people in business in this country, I shall not be doing it any more." He started selling off his assets and will have all of his assets sold by the end of 1994. He said: "My reasons for not staying in business: GST, fines, withholding tax reporting, government operating and regulating at the same time, such as UIC, WCB, no offsetting write-offs when a deal goes bad and abuse by Revenue Canada. I have one big
Adjournment Debate
problem in business: government, government, government! Yours sincerely, Mr. Lou MacEachem."
I appreciate the minister doing his best to put me in an awkward light by saying that Mr. MacEachem was not leaving the country.
There are 900,000 entrepreneurs in this country right now. They are begging this government to listen. What they want the government to hear is that the paper burden and the tax designs of this government are crushing their entrepreneurial spirit. Tomorrow is an emergency debate on small business and so we can continue this discussion then.

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles A. Langlois (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened with great interest to what was said by the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood. Perhaps I may remind him that his party, which was in power for many years before this government was elected, put a very heavy burden on small businesses and on Canadian business in general.
The hon. member has, I believe, a business background. I am sure there were good times and times when things were not so good. He must admit that government tax burdens and red tape did not start in 1984 or 1988. It started well before that time. The hon. member knows the business community. He must have realized, and his friends must have told him, that since 1984, this government has been working very hard to enhance the position of Canada's small businesses. It has introduced policies to help Canadian small businesses become more competitive and more actively involved in export markets.

My colleague will remember that not too long ago we replaced the old manufacturers' sales tax with a new tax, the GST. The GST being a different tax is not a new tax. It replaces the tax that put a burden on our economy, on the capacity of our small business to compete and to export.
As my colleague said, tomorrow there is a special debate on this issue. I am sure that all members of this House will welcome the opportunity to talk about it.

October 10, 1991
Adjournment Debate POVERTY

Madam Speaker, I have the opportunity this evening to rise in response to a question that I posed in this House to the Prime Minister on October 2 that had to do with the rate of child poverty in this country.
I thought perhaps at the time that the Prime Minister had unintentionally misconstrued what I was asking in my question because of the response I got from him in which he said I was trying to mislead the Canadian public and was giving false information.
I tabled information in this House which corroborated the statement I made which was that there are more than one million children living in poverty in this country. I say that I thought that perhaps I had been misinterpreted and gave the Prime Minister the benefit of the doubt. I was frankly appalled by a response I got to my question from the Minister of National Health and Welfare in which he critiqued what I had said in the document that had been tabled in the House.
Subsequently I have been in touch with many of the agencies that deal with those living in poverty in this country and particularly children. In 1990 Statistics Canada tells us that there were 5.6 million children under the age of 14 years living in Canada. Those human beings who are aged 15, 16, 17 and 18 are also considered to be children in this country. One in six children today is estimated to be living in poverty in this country. That makes more than one million children living in poverty in this country. It is a dreadful legacy that we leave for the future of this country to permit such a thing to exist.
Beyond just the argument over statistics and numbers, I was very concerned with what the Minister of National Health and Welfare was saying in his letter. At one point he stated that we should be proud of certain statistics about Canadian initiatives and other federal initiatives that have been taken vis-a-vis children.
For example, the government has made a dollar commitment to eliminating the problem of family violence. That is very important and we support that. We know that the situation of poverty contributes to family violence in this country and the government is not facing the reality of how children are living in this country.
I certainly am affronted by the response and the attitude of this government. It is not only myself. There
are many people who care for children and their future in this country and our country's future is our children today. The government will hear more from me and those agencies on this issue in the coming days.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I believe that in his exchange with the hon. member for Northumberland, the Prime Minister mentioned major programs the government has launched in response to this appalling situation that affects us all, both intellectually and emotionally: the thousands of children living in poverty in this country.
I heard her refer to a letter she received from the minister with further details on the government's initiatives. Of course, it is quite a challenge, and it is also a very complex issue that is difficult to quantify when we realize, for instance, that there are poor children who are fortunate: they eat three meals a day, are cherished by their parents, cared for and protected. These children may be poor, but they are not unhappy. On the other hand, there are poor children who lead miserable lives because they come from a disadvantaged environment, broken homes, families living in extreme poverty, where many of them are beaten and abused. Single-parent families are most likely to be living on low incomes, and the children in these families are particularly exposed to poverty.
Madam Speaker, I know the hon. member doesn't like figures, but I think I should mention a few, because the government spends $15 billion annually on aid to children through family assistance programs. The hon. member is aware there are provincial jurisdictions involved as well. At the present time, there are 956,000 fewer low-income people than in 1984.1 agree we must do more. We are very concerned, Madam Speaker, and we are actively seeking ways to improve our response to the needs of these children. It will take the co-operation of both opposition members and the government to find short and medium-term solutions to this very serious problem facing our society.
